strengths: Clear and well-motivated framing: casting auxiliary classification as representation selection over the full L×T×d hidden-state tensor, connecting the deployment-oriented question of 'where to read out' to classical BERTology findings about layer-wise specialization

Comprehensive empirical coverage across two task settings (safety moderation on ToxicChat and WildGuardMix, including a cross-dataset/OOD transfer setting, and sentiment/emotion on IMDB, SST-2, Emotion), with a sensible spectrum of probe complexity (pooling → scoring attention → downcast MHA) enabling controlled comparisons

Consistent method ranking across datasets and tasks (pooling < scoring attention < MHA) with error bars over 3 runs on several results, which supports the central claim that learned token–layer aggregation outperforms fixed readouts and logit-only reuse (MULI)

Strong systems-oriented evaluation: end-to-end latency, throughput, and peak VRAM comparisons against a guard-then-serve pipeline (Table 5) directly quantify the practical deployment benefit, which is the paper's main selling point

Good supporting material: ~100-configuration hyperparameter search with sensitivity analysis (Appendix A, Figure 3), downcasting ablation (Table 7) showing most gains come from where features are read rather than capacity, and layer-weight visualizations on two tasks (Figures 2, 4)

Honest and thorough limitations section covering single-backbone generalization, sequence length, data requirements, inherited biases, and the detect-only (non-explanatory) nature of the approach, plus an ethics discussion
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the technical components: the scoring-attention gate is essentially attention pooling and the MHA probe is a standard downcast transformer block; the main contribution is the two-stage token–layer aggregation template and its evaluation, which is an incremental combination of known probing techniques

Single backbone evaluation (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct only). The authors acknowledge this, but the core BERTology-style claim (that task-relevant signals are distributed across depth in decoder-only LLMs and that learned aggregation is needed) would be substantially more convincing with at least one additional model family or size

Baseline comparisons are not fully controlled: guard models in Tables 2–3 come from other papers with different architectures, training data, and prompts, so several key comparisons are indicative rather than head-to-head; no reuse-baseline with matched backbone other than MULI, and ShieldHead is reported on different backbones (8B/27B)

Some interpretive overreach: the layer-attention analysis (Section 5) treats probe attention weights as evidence about where safety features emerge, but attention weights are a mechanism of the probe, not a direct measure of feature location; the claim of a 'common ancestor representation' in Section 2 is asserted rather than tested (e.g., no cross-task probing or shared-layer transfer experiment)

Reproducibility gaps: the code-availability footnote appears incomplete (empty URL), exact train/validation splits and prompt templates for the LLM forward pass are not described, some tables report single values without variance (e.g., Table 2), and per-dataset selected hyperparameter configurations are referenced but only ranges are shown in the appendix

Missing error analysis on the safety tasks (per-category breakdown on WildGuardMix harm types, false-positive/false-negative trade-offs at matched operating points), which matters for a moderation application; AUPRC is omitted for several guard baselines, complicating threshold-free comparison

strengths: The problem is practically relevant: reducing the latency, VRAM, and orchestration cost of separate guard models by reusing the serving LLM's forward pass is a real deployment concern, and the paper frames it clearly.

The systems-level evaluation (Table 5: throughput, latency, peak GPU memory for probe-attached serving vs. guard-then-serve) is a valuable and unusually concrete contribution that most probing papers omit.

The experimental pipeline is reasonably thorough: ~100 hyperparameter configurations per dataset, sensitivity analysis (Figure 3), a downcasting ablation (Table 7) with 3-run means and standard deviations, and qualitative layer-attention analysis on two tasks (Figures 2 and 4).

Results across five benchmarks show a consistent ranking of the three aggregation mechanisms (pooling < scoring attention < MHA), and the MHA probe is competitive with much larger guard models while adding only ~35M parameters.
The paper is generally well organized, the architecture is simple and easy to follow, and a Limitations section candidly acknowledges the single-backbone constraint and other gaps.
Code availability and detailed hyperparameter ranges in the appendix support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claim — that learned token-and-layer selection beats committing to a fixed layer or token — is not directly substantiated by a controlled baseline. The most important missing control is a probe on a single fixed layer (especially last-layer mean pooling), which is the de facto standard readout. MULI (first-token logits) and ShieldHead (final-layer head) are cited from prior work rather than run under matched conditions, so the paper cannot cleanly isolate the benefit of joint L×T selection versus simply reading the last layer well.

Missing comparison to low-cost fine-tuning alternatives (e.g., LoRA on the serving model, or a lightly fine-tuned classification head) that also avoid a separate guard model and could match the reported accuracy; without this, the compute-accuracy trade-off is not fully characterized.

Single backbone only (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct). All layer-related conclusions (e.g., 'safety signals emerge around L17') may be architecture- and scale-specific; the authors acknowledge this but a second backbone (even 1B or 8B in the same family) would have materially strengthened the claims.

Several headline comparisons are cross-paper and cross-dataset (Tables 2 and 3 mix guard models trained on different data, numbers taken from other papers) and the authors themselves call them 'indicative rather than controlled head-to-head matches'; no statistical significance testing is reported for the key deltas.

Limited novelty: two-stage attention/pooling aggregation over hidden states is a natural combination of well-known components, and probing single or multiple layers of LLMs is well explored (Di Palma et al. 2025, ShieldHead, OmniGuard, Zhou et al. 2024). The 'BERTology' framing is largely motivational; the analysis in Section 5 is descriptive (attention weight histograms) rather than establishing a new mechanistic insight.
The '35M parameter' MHA probe strains the 'lightweight probe' narrative, and the cost of training-time caching of all L×T×d hidden states (storage, preprocessing) is mentioned only briefly.

Writing has a number of small errors ('an model invocation', the garbled 'There must be for each task, a common ancestor representation that is useful for both' sentence), and Figure 1's caption/depiction of the pipeline is somewhat confusing.

The out-of-distribution result (Table 2) shows direct pooling collapsing to 53.33 F1, which raises questions about when the simplest probes can be trusted in deployment; the paper does not provide guidance on probe selection or failure modes for practitioners.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant deployment problem: reusing the serving LLM's forward pass for moderation/classification rather than paying for a separate guard model, which is a timely orchestration question for production NLP systems.

The core framing — treating classification as representation selection over the full L×T×d hidden-state tensor rather than committing to a fixed token or layer — is a clean and sensible generalization of prior fixed-readout approaches (MULI, ShieldHead, OmniGuard), well motivated by BERTology literature.

Evaluation spans five benchmarks across two settings (safety and sentiment/emotion), including a cross-dataset (out-of-distribution) transfer test (WildGuardMix → ToxicChat) that strengthens the safety claims.

The paper is commendably transparent about deployment trade-offs: it groups baselines by whether an extra LM call is required, reports added parameters beyond the backbone, and provides an end-to-end latency/throughput/VRAM benchmark (Table 5) showing ~4.5–6x latency reduction versus a guard-then-serve pipeline.

Good ablation and sensitivity work: ~100 configurations per dataset with sensitivity analysis (Fig. 3), a downcasting ablation (Table 7), and class-conditional layer-weight visualizations (Figs. 2 and 4) that connect the architecture to the interpretability motivation.

Consistent results with reported standard deviations across runs, and results are generally strong: MHA probe (88.55 F1 on WildGuardMix, 84.51 F1 on ToxicChat) approaches or exceeds guard baselines with orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters than guard LLMs.
weaknesses: Single backbone: all results use Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. The claim that signals generalize or scale to larger/deployed models is acknowledged as a hypothesis but never tested, which limits the headline claim of practical deployment value.

A critical missing ablation: the central claim is that learned token–layer aggregation beats committing to a fixed layer or token, but there is no controlled comparison against a simple probe on (a) final-layer mean pooling, or (b) the best single layer selected on validation data. Comparisons to ShieldHead/OmniGuard are borrowed numbers from other papers with different backbones and training data, so the 'where to read' claim is supported only indirectly.

Baseline comparability concerns: most baseline numbers are transplanted from prior work (potentially different splits, prompts, or metrics), and the authors' own probes receive an extensive ~100-configuration hyperparameter search that the baselines did not. The paper flags cross-dataset comparisons as 'indicative' but the tuning asymmetry applies everywhere.
Reproducibility gap: the code URL in Section 4.1 is empty ('Code available at' with no link), so the results cannot currently be independently reproduced.

The token-selection half of the story is underexplored: the analysis (Section 5, Appendix C) only visualizes layer-level aggregation weights; there is no equivalent analysis or ablation for the token-level gate, leaving half the 'token×layer' contribution empirically unsubstantiated.

The MHA probe is not as lightweight as the narrative suggests — 35M trainable parameters and a meaningful latency cost (24.8 vs 37.8 samples/s baseline) — and the ablation shows 283M-parameter variants that complicate the parameter-efficiency framing; this is disclosed but deserves more critical discussion.

Writing and presentation issues: the opaque sentence 'There must be for each task, a common ancestor representation that is useful for both', a missing footnote URL, and minor grammatical errors ('require an model invocation') reduce polish.

Statistical rigor is modest: 3-run means ± std in the ablation, but no significance tests for the headline comparisons, some of which are within ~1–2 points of strong baselines (e.g., 88.55 vs WildGuard 88.9; 84.51 vs 82.2).

strengths: Practically relevant problem: reusing the serving LLM's forward pass for auxiliary classification addresses real latency/VRAM/deployment costs in LLM orchestration, with a clearly stated thesis (learn where to read out over tokens and layers rather than committing to a fixed token/layer).

Comprehensive empirical validation: five datasets spanning safety and sentiment, three backbones including two mixture-of-experts architectures, and a consistent method ranking (pooling < scoring attention < MHA) across all backbones, which supports the generalization claim.
Useful systems-level evaluation: the latency/throughput/peak-memory benchmark (Table 5) directly quantifies the guard-then-serve vs. single-pass trade-off, which most probing papers omit.

Transparent hyperparameter reporting (~100 configurations per dataset, full search ranges in Table 6), sensitivity analysis over PR-AUC (Figure 3), and a downcasting ablation (Table 7) that supports the claim that gains come from where signals are read, not from added capacity.

The layer-attention analysis (Figures 2 and 4) connects the learned aggregation to BERTology findings with interpretable class-conditional depth profiles, giving qualitative insight beyond raw accuracy numbers.
Candid limitations section acknowledging OOD degradation, silent-failure risk, sequence-length constraints, and missing evaluation of refusal generation.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method is essentially attention pooling over tokens and layers applied to hidden states; multi-layer aggregation and learned readout probing are well-established (Tenney et al., Jawahar et al., de Vries et al.), and the contribution is more a well-executed engineering instantiations than a new technique.

The 'single-pass alongside generation' framing is only benchmarked with max_new_tokens=1 (Table 5 caption), so the true serving cost when the model generates longer outputs (repeated forward passes, KV-cache interplay, and the cost of exposing all L×T×d hidden states) is not fully characterized. Anomalies in Table 5 (all probe rows appear faster than the base model, 23.72–24.93 vs. 26.43 ms) suggest measurement noise or missing overhead accounting (e.g., materializing hidden states) that is not explained.

Baseline comparability is mixed: several guard-model/API numbers in Tables 2–4 are imported from prior papers under differing architectures and training data (acknowledged as 'indicative'), and it is unclear whether MULI was retrained or cited per setting; a controlled head-to-head under identical training data is missing for the headline claims.

No statistical significance testing; results are mean±std over 3 runs, and some reported gaps (e.g., SST-2 and IMDB within ~0.5 points between MHA and standalone classifiers) are too small to support strong claims.

Reproducibility is undermined by an incomplete code link (footnote 1 reads 'Code available at' with no URL), and no release of cached hidden states, seeds, or exact selected configurations for the additional backbones.

Safety impact is limited relative to guard models: probes only detect and cannot generate refusals or reasoning, degrade under OOD shift (direct pooling drops to 53.33 F1), and may silently fail on novel jailbreaks — acknowledged but meaningfully tempering the claimed replacement of the guard-model pipeline.

Scale generalization is untested: all three backbones have ~3B active parameters, so the paper's own argument that stronger backbones improve relative probe accuracy remains conjecture, as the limitations section concedes.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: reusing the serving LLM's forward pass for moderation/sentiment classification instead of deploying a separate guard model, which is a real orchestration concern.

Empirical coverage is reasonably broad for this line of work: five datasets spanning safety and sentiment, three backbones including two mixture-of-experts architectures, a latency/VRAM benchmark comparing guard-then-serve pipelines, an ablation on attention downcasting (Table 7), and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (~100 configs, Figure 3).

Results are reported as mean ± std over 3 runs, and the method ranking (pooling < scoring attention < MHA) is consistent across all three backbones, which lends credibility to the comparative claims within the probe family.

The paper is generally well written, and the Limitations section is unusually candid (acknowledging sequence-length constraints, OOD degradation, single-model-family coverage for sentiment, and the lack of explanatory rejection generation).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. Learned aggregation over hidden states is a small delta over existing reuse methods (MULI, ShieldHead, LPM, OmniGuard, and prior multi-layer probing/BERTology work that the paper itself cites). The two-stage token-then-layer aggregator is essentially attention pooling over a tensor; the 'BERTology' framing is mostly narrative rather than a substantive analytic contribution.

Several headline comparisons are not controlled. Standalone guard/classifier baselines (Tables 1, 2, 4) are imported from prior papers with different training data, prompting protocols, and architectures; the paper concedes these are 'indicative' only, yet the abstract claims probes 'match or surpass substantially larger task-specific baselines.' Under matched training data, the picture is less favorable.

Out-of-distribution results undercut the strong claims: on ToxicChat trained on WildGuardMix, direct pooling drops to 53.33 F1 and the best probe reaches 72.88 F1 vs. 82.2 for ToxicChat-T5. The probes are also acknowledged to fail silently on novel harm categories, a serious concern for the safety deployment story.

The layer-attention analysis (Figure 2) treats the probe's softmax attention weights as an explanation of where features live. Attention weights are well known to be an unreliable proxy for importance, so the 'BERTology' conclusions about which layers encode safety signals are descriptive at best and under-supported.

Reproducibility is undermined: footnote 1 reads 'Code available at' with no URL or repository, and no release commitment appears elsewhere. Without code, the ~100-configuration hyperparameter search and probe training cannot be reliably replicated.

The efficiency benchmark (Table 5) uses batch size 1 and max_new_tokens=1, which favors the probe-heavy single-pass setup and does not reflect realistic batched serving; the comparison to guard models that could run concurrently is therefore not fully convincing.

Gains over the simplest reuse baseline are sometimes marginal (e.g., Emotion 87.68 vs. MULI 64.05 is large, but IMDB/SST-2 gains over MULI and over DeBERTa/RoBERTa are within ~1 point of strong baselines), and no statistical significance testing is reported to support the ordering claims.

The MHA probe at 27–35M trainable parameters stretches the 'lightweight probe' framing, and the paper does not clearly justify why an attention stack over all layers/tokens is preferable to cheaper alternatives (e.g., learned layer weights over last-token states) beyond the three variants tested.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated problem framing: reusing the serving LLM's forward pass for auxiliary classification (moderation and NLU) addresses a real deployment concern (latency, VRAM, orchestration complexity), and the paper connects it nicely to the BERTology literature on layer-wise information.

Comprehensive and mostly well-controlled empirical study: three backbones spanning dense and MoE architectures (Llama-3.2-3B, GPT-OSS-20B, Qwen3-30B-A3B), five datasets covering safety and sentiment, and a consistent method ranking (pooling < scoring attention < MHA) across settings.

Honest baseline grouping: the paper explicitly distinguishes standalone classifiers requiring an extra LM call from same-pass reuse methods, and reports added parameter counts separately, which makes the deployment trade-off transparent rather than conflating accuracy with system cost.

Practical systems evaluation (Table 5): end-to-end latency, throughput, and peak memory comparisons against guard-then-serve pipelines with three real guard models substantiate the central efficiency claim, not just parameter counts.

Good reproducibility support: hyperparameter search ranges, ~100 configurations per dataset, hardware details, sensitivity/violin analyses (Figure 3), and a downcasting ablation (Table 7) with mean ± std over 3 runs.
Interpretability analysis (Figures 2 and 4) provides class-conditional layer-attention profiles that support the 'distributed signal' motivation and add qualitative insight beyond aggregate metrics.
Clear writing, thorough related work, and a candid Limitations section (OOD degradation, sequence-length constraints, data-size requirements, single-pass detection-only limitation).
weaknesses: Limited novelty in methodology: attention pooling over tokens/layers and lightweight probes on hidden states are well-established techniques; the contribution is primarily an empirical/systems packaging of known components rather than a new method. The two-stage aggregation framing is sensible but architecturally simple.

The central claim — that learned token-layer aggregation beats committing to a fixed layer or token — is not directly ablated within the paper's own framework. There is no 'probe at each single layer' sweep or 'fixed random/last-layer pooling with the same head' control, so the advantage over a well-chosen fixed layer (not just first-token logits as in MULI) is not isolated.

Several headline comparisons are not controlled head-to-head: Table 2 guard baselines are cited from prior work with different training data and architectures, which the authors acknowledge ('indicative rather than controlled'); conclusions like 'outperform several guard baselines' should be read cautiously.

Out-of-distribution degradation is substantial (e.g., pooling drops to 53.33 F1 on cross-dataset ToxicChat), and the paper does not evaluate robustness to adversarial jailbreak-style shifts at inference time, which matters for the safety use case it targets.

The MHA probe is 35M parameters, which is no longer obviously 'lightweight' relative to the 3B backbone and weakens the parameter-efficiency narrative relative to the scoring-attention gate (0.10M) that comes close in some settings; the trade-off discussion is present but could be sharper.
Statistical significance of the gaps (e.g., 84.51 vs 80.49 F1 on ToxicChat, or vs. the 82.2 standalone baseline) is not tested; only std over 3 runs is reported.

Reproducibility gaps: the code footnote appears to have no actual URL; memory footprint of caching the full L×T×d hidden states for training (especially for longer sequences) is not quantified, though the Limitations section concedes sequence-length constraints.

Some claims lean on external expectations rather than evidence, e.g., the scaling-law argument that probe accuracy would improve 'relatively unachanged' with stronger backbones is asserted rather than tested (all backbones are ~3B active).
